full_text_en:
**Huzhou Huitai Garment Co., Ltd. v. Dalian Huaxun International Air Freight Co., Ltd., Ningbo Branch**  
— Retrial case concerning dispute over international air cargo transportation freight  

**Retrial Applicant**: Huzhou Huitai Garment Co., Ltd., Zhejiang Province.  
**Legal Representative**: Wu Jiangen, Chairman of the Board.  
**Agent ad litem**: Wang Yingbo, Attorney at Beijing Shanghai Law Firm.  

**Opposing Party**: Dalian Huaxun International Air Freight Co., Ltd., Ningbo Branch.  
**Legal Representative**: Li Le, Manager.  

The retrial applicant, Huzhou Huitai Garment Co., Ltd., Zhejiang Province (hereinafter referred to as "Huitai Company"), dissatisfied with the civil judgment (1995) Zhe Jing Zhong Zi No. 321 of the Zhejiang High People's Court in the dispute over international air cargo transportation freight with Dalian Huaxun International Air Freight Co., Ltd., Ningbo Branch (hereinafter referred to as "Huaxun Company"), applied for a retrial to the Supreme People's Court. Upon review, the Supreme People's Court held that the original judgment had insufficient evidence for the facts found and improperly applied the law, and decided to bring the case for trial under Articles 179(1)(ii) and (iii) and Article 183 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC.  

Upon trial, the Supreme People's Court found the following facts:  

In early 1993, Chen Weiming (Italian name: MinGo), an Italian agent, entered into a silk garment trade contract with the retrial applicant, Huitai Company. The trade terms under the contract were FOB Shanghai. On April 23 of the same year, Chen Weiming entered into a "Consignment Transport Contract" with International Freight Consultants S.r.l., Milan Branch (hereinafter referred to as "I.F.C. Company"), stipulating that I.F.C. Company would handle the transportation of imported goods from China to Italy for Chen Weiming. Chen Weiming entrusted all import goods to I.F.C. Company for exclusive carriage and agreed not to transfer them to any other agent. Chen Weiming would deliver the goods exported from China to He Suifeng, the person in charge of I.F.C. Company's office in China, who was required to ship the received goods to Italy within one week and ensure no delivery delay occurred. Upon arrival of the goods in Milan, Chen Weiming had to immediately pay the freight to I.F.C. Company before taking delivery; otherwise, Chen Weiming would also pay warehouse storage fees. After the contract was signed, on April 29 of the same year, Chen Weiming faxed Zhongfa Company, the intermediary of Huitai Company, informing Huitai Company that this and future export goods should be shipped by I.F.C. Company, with freight to be paid upon pickup in Milan, and provided the address of He Suifeng, the person in charge of I.F.C. Company's office in China, in Hangzhou, requesting Huitai Company to contact her promptly to arrange export procedures. For ease of booking cargo space and shipment, Huitai Company, as requested by He Suifeng, used the "International Cargo Consignment Note" of China Eastern Airlines (hereinafter "CEA"), faxing the completed consignment note to He Suifeng. He Suifeng delivered the consignment note to Huaxun Company, CEA's sales agent. Between May and September of the same year, Huitai Company delivered goods seven times to Huaxun Company's warehouse at Shanghai Hongqiao Airport as instructed by He Suifeng. Huaxun Company signed for the goods, then completed and issued six CEA master air waybills and entrusted Huali Air Freight Co., Ltd., Shanghai Branch, to issue one master air waybill for Air China. The six master air waybills issued by Huaxun Company recorded the shipper as Huaxun Company and the consignee as GONDRAND Company in Brussels, Belgium. The master air waybill issued by Huali Air Freight Co., Ltd., Shanghai Branch, recorded the consignee as I.F.C. Milan. Huaxun Company also issued seven house air waybills. The house air waybills recorded the shipper as Huitai Company and the consignees as the various Italian customers designated by Huitai Company in the consignment note. During this period, Huaxun Company, in accordance with the airline's requirement for prepayment of freight, paid CEA and Huali Air Freight Co., Ltd., Shanghai Branch, a total of RMB 449,311.50 in air freight for the seven shipments (six payments for Shanghai-Brussels air freight and one for Shanghai-Milan air freight). After the goods were dispatched, Huaxun Company did not deliver the original shipper copy of the house air waybill to Huitai Company, nor did it demand air freight from Huitai Company. The seven shipments arrived in Milan successively between May and September of the same year. Chen Weiming paid the full air and land freight to I.F.C. Milan and took delivery of the goods, along with I.F.C. clearance fees and miscellaneous charges. I.F.C. Milan issued invoices and receipts, stating that the carriage contract for these goods had been fully performed. On February 10, 1995, Huaxun Company sent a letter to Huitai Company stating: "At that time, Huitai Company entrusted I.F.C. Company; now I.F.C. Company has transferred its right to collect payment to Huaxun Company," and demanded that Huitai Company pay the full air freight of USD 101,712.824 for the seven shipments from Shanghai to Milan according to the house air waybills. Huitai Company refused on the grounds that the freight was to be paid by the foreign buyer and that it had no obligation to pay. A dispute arose. Huaxun Company then filed a lawsuit in the Huzhou Intermediate People's Court, Zhejiang Province, demanding that Huitai Company pay the full air freight and late fees as recorded in the house air waybills, totaling USD 126,123.904.  

The Huzhou Intermediate People's Court held that although the parties had not signed a written consignment transport contract, Huitai Company had delivered the goods to Huaxun Company's warehouse and signed the cargo consignment note; Huaxun Company had transported the goods to the destination and was entitled to collect freight from Huitai Company. Huitai Company's argument that the foreign buyer would pay the freight was unfounded. The court therefore ordered Huitai Company to pay Huaxun Company freight and overdue liquidated damages totaling USD 126,123.904. Huitai Company appealed to the Zhejiang High People's Court.  

In the second instance, the Zhejiang High People's Court held that although no written consignment transport contract had been signed, Huitai Company exported the goods in its own name, delivered them to Huaxun Company's warehouse, and signed the cargo consignment note for confirmation; Huaxun Company had entrusted the airline to transport the goods to the location designated by Huitai Company for delivery. The consignment transport relationship between the parties should be deemed established. Huaxun Company had performed its consignment transport obligations, and Huitai Company should pay the freight. The consignment transport contract between the Italian customer and I.F.C. Company was unrelated to this case. The court dismissed Huitai Company's appeal and affirmed the first-instance judgment.  

In the retrial, the Supreme People's Court held:  

According to the trade terms agreed between Italian agent Chen Weiming and Huitai Company, it was the buyer's obligation to conclude the transport contract and pay the freight. Accordingly, Chen Weiming and I.F.C. Milan entered into the "Consignment Transport Contract," the content of which indicated that I.F.C. Company was the contracting carrier for the seven shipments and Chen Weiming was the shipper. Since I.F.C. Company did not have the qualification to operate international freight forwarding business in the exporting country, China, and to ensure that the goods in this case could be timely booked with the airline for shipment and, as instructed by Chen Weiming, transshipped via Brussels to Milan, I.F.C. Company had to entrust international freight forwarders in Shanghai, China, and Brussels, Belgium, to assist in completing the local transport. The master air waybills in this case recorded the shipper as Huaxun Company and the consignee as GONDRAND Company. GONDRAND Company was the I.F.C. Company's entrusted export agent in the country of dispatch and transshipment agent. According to GONDRAND Company's testimony, it handled the transport of the goods in this case via Brussels to Milan as entrusted by I.F.C. Company, and the expenses incurred, including customs duties, tax agency fees, air cargo pickup fees, documentation fees, and truck freight, were all paid by I.F.C. Company to GONDRAND Company, which never dealt directly with the cargo owner; all instructions came from I.F.C. Company. The financial matters between GONDRAND Company and I.F.C. Company had been fully settled. The issue of domestic freight in China was irrelevant to GONDRAND Company and should be resolved with the Italian I.F.C. Company. The practice of GONDRAND Company accepting entrustment from I.F.C. Company and settling fees with I.F.C. Company is a common practice in international air cargo forwarding where forwarders handle FOB (FCA) goods transport on behalf of each other. As I.F.C. Company's export agent, the air freight paid by Huaxun Company to the airline should also be collected from I.F.C. Company. Although Huitai Company delivered the goods to Huaxun Company's warehouse at Shanghai Hongqiao Airport and its name was filled in the "Shipper" column of the house air waybill, this cannot be taken as establishing a consignment transport relationship between the two parties. According to the "Consignment Transport Contract," Huitai Company was required to deliver the goods to I.F.C. Company. Delivering the goods to Huaxun Company's warehouse was an act performed by Huitai Company as instructed by I.F.C. Company, not a consignment to Huaxun Company. Huitai Company was merely the person delivering the goods to I.F.C. Company as directed by Chen Weiming. Huaxun Company accepted the goods, but as I.F.C. Company's export agent, it filled out the air waybill and shipped the goods to the airline, which was not a consignment received from Huitai Company. It was an act of transporting the goods received from I.F.C. Company to the airline. According to Article 11(1) of the Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules Relating to International Carriage by Air (the Warsaw Convention), to which China is a party: "The air waybill shall be *prima facie* evidence of the conclusion of the contract, of the receipt of the goods and of the conditions of carriage." Although Huaxun Company, as CEA's sales agent, issued the air waybill, there is contrary evidence in this case showing that Chen Weiming and I.F.C. Milan performed the "Consignment Transport Contract" with respect to payment of air freight and delivery of goods, thereby negating the evidentiary effect of the house air waybill as a contract. The house air waybill served only as a receipt evidencing that I.F.C. Company had received and shipped the goods in this case. Furthermore, after successively dispatching the goods between May and September 1993, Huaxun Company never delivered the original shipper copy of the house air waybill (the transport contract document) to Huitai Company, and only demanded freight from Huitai Company 15 to 21 months later. This practice, which violates the relevant provisions of the Warsaw Convention and does not conform to industry practices in international air freight forwarding, also indicates that Huaxun Company did not consider itself to have a consignment transport relationship with Huitai Company.  

Huaxun Company's claim for freight from Huitai Company on the ground that I.F.C. Company had transferred its right to collect payment is also untenable. The evidence in this case shows that I.F.C. Company had already received the full freight from Chen Weiming, the transport contract had been fully performed, and the right to collect payment no longer existed. Moreover, changing the party obligated to pay freight based on an agency relationship between freight forwarders violates the trade terms agreed upon by the parties to the trade contract. Therefore, the so-called transfer of the right to collect payment is invalid against Huitai Company.  

Huaxun Company argued in its defense that, according to the "Several Provisions on the Administration of International Freight Forwarding Industry" promulgated by the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation of China in 1990, I.F.C. Company could not solicit cargo or subcontract to agents within China, thereby denying its agency relationship with I.F.C. Company. However, Article 8(3) of the said MOFTEC document provides that international freight forwarding enterprises "may accept entrustment from foreign freight forwarders to handle consolidation, consignment, LCL, container packing/unpacking, warehousing, distribution, transshipment, door-to-door transport, express delivery, and consulting services." In this case, I.F.C. Company solicited Chen Weiming's import goods in Italy and entrusted a Chinese international freight forwarder to handle the consignment and export, which fully complies with the provisions of the MOFTEC document and is also a common practice in the international air freight forwarding industry. The consignees designated by Huitai Company in this case were various Italian customers, not I.F.C. Company or GONDRAND Company. The relationship between I.F.C. Company, Huaxun Company, and GONDRAND Company is one of air freight agency, which does not involve the cargo owner. The full freight for the seven shipments in this case should be collected by I.F.C. Milan from Chen Weiming, and I.F.C. Company should reimburse Huaxun Company and GONDRAND Company for the prepaid air freight and transshipment costs, respectively, based on the agency relationship. The air freight paid by Huaxun Company to the airline was a prepayment on behalf of I.F.C. Company and should be reimbursed by I.F.C. Company. If I.F.C. Company fails to reimburse, it constitutes a commercial risk, and Huaxun Company cannot assert rights under a so-called "assignment of rights" to the detriment of a third party. Moreover, the freight claimed by Huaxun Company is the full air freight from Shanghai via Brussels to Milan as recorded in the house air waybill, which includes expenses payable by I.F.C. Company to GONDRAND Company and expenses incurred by I.F.C. Company in Milan, clearly exceeding the air freight Huaxun Company paid to the airline under the master air waybill. Huaxun Company failed to provide a reasonable explanation for this.  

In summary, in accordance with Articles 179(1)(ii) and (iii) of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, the Supreme People's Court ruled on April 9, 1997:  

1. The second-instance civil judgment of the Zhejiang High People's Court and the first-instance civil judgment of the Huzhou Intermediate People's Court are hereby reversed.  

2. Huaxun Company's lawsuit is dismissed.  

Court acceptance fees for the first and second instances of RMB 67,706, and litigation preservation fees of RMB 5,000, shall be borne by Huaxun Company.
